title: Fetch, Storage, and Other Web APIs
summary: Talk to servers with fetch, take over forms, store data in the browser, change the URL without reloading, and meet the other APIs browsers give you.
intro: A page that only changes itself can't do much. Real pages show fresh data without reloading, save what you type without leaving, remember your settings for next time, and keep an address you can share that opens the same view. Each of those is a Web API, one of the features the browser gives your JavaScript, which you met in the lesson on how a browser draws a page. This lesson covers the ones you'll use on almost every project: fetch for talking to servers, forms that send in the background, the browser's rules about which servers a page may read from, the places a page can store data, the URL and the History API, and a quick tour of the rest, from timers to code that runs on another thread.

steps.title: Fetching data

examples.title: The notes server
examples.prompt: Save this as server.mjs in the notes-app folder and start it with node server.mjs. It keeps its notes in memory, so they reset when you stop it with Ctrl+C.
examples.explanation: You only need the outline. `createServer` takes a function that Node.js calls for every request, much like an event listener, and it prints each request's method and path in the terminal, so you can watch your page's requests arrive. A GET to `/api/notes` answers with the notes as JSON, keeping only those that contain the `q` in the query string, if there is one. A POST to `/api/notes` reads a JSON body with a `text`, saves the note, and answers `201 Created` with it, or `400 Bad Request` when the body is wrong. Anything else is a file from `public`, or a 404. `server.listen` starts it on port 8000, private to your computer, just like Python's server. The backend courses explain every line.

examples.title: A first fetch
examples.prompt: Saved as public/app.js, loaded by public/index.html as a module, with the server running. The page was opened at http://localhost:8000/.
examples.output:
The request has started, and the script carries on.
200 true
application/json
2 Bring water
examples.explanation: The last line printed first. Calling `showNotes()` runs it as far as the first `await`, where it pauses and returns, so the script's next line runs right away. When the response arrives, `showNotes` picks up where it stopped: the status is 200, so `ok` is `true`, and the `Content-Type` header says JSON. The second `await` waits for the body and parses it into an array of two note objects. `/api/notes` is a path with no host, so it goes to the page's own server, the same way a relative link does. Watch the server's terminal while you reload, and you'll see `GET /api/notes` arrive after `GET /app.js`.

examples.title: A 404 is still a response
examples.prompt: The same page asks for a note the server doesn't have. These are the lines the script printed.
examples.output:
404 false
Couldn't load note 99: The server answered 404
examples.explanation: The server has no address `/api/notes/99`, so it answers 404. `fetch` doesn't reject: the server answered, so the first `await` gives a response, with `ok` set to `false`. The `if` turns that into an error with `throw`, which skips the rest of the `try` block, so `note.text` never runs, and the `catch` block gets the error, whose `message` is the text you gave it. Without the check, the code would go on to read the server's error body as if it were a note. The Console also shows the failed request in red by itself, with its address and the 404, which is handy while you work.

steps.title: Sending data, and taking over forms
steps.body:
Reading data is half the job. The other half is sending it: a comment, a saved setting, an item for the cart. Forms send data too, but by default a submit loads a whole new page, as the forms lesson showed. With `fetch`, a page can send in the background, stay where it is, and show the result in place.

## Sending JSON

`fetch` takes a second argument, an object of **options**:

```javascript
const response = await fetch("/api/notes", {
  method: "POST",
  headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" },
  body: JSON.stringify({ text: "Pack snacks" }),
});
```

`method` is the HTTP method, GET when you leave it out. `headers` adds request headers, and `Content-Type` tells the server the body is JSON. `body` is what you send, as text, so `JSON.stringify` turns the object into JSON first. The notes server answers `201 Created`, with the saved note as JSON, which you read with `await response.json()` as before.

## Taking over a form

Listen for the form's `submit` event and call `event.preventDefault()`, from the previous lesson, so the browser doesn't send it the usual way. Then read the fields with **FormData**:

```javascript
const data = new FormData(form);
const text = data.get("text");
```

`new FormData(form)` collects every field by its `name` attribute, the same names and values the browser would have sent, so `get("text")` is what's in the field called `text`. For a form with many fields, `Object.fromEntries(data)` makes them one plain object, ready for `JSON.stringify`.

A FormData can also be the `body` itself. The browser then sends it as `multipart/form-data`, the format forms use for files, and sets the `Content-Type` for you, so don't set it yourself. Use whichever the server expects. The notes server reads JSON.

## Let the browser check first

The checks from the forms lesson, like `required`, `minlength`, and `type="email"`, still run. If a field fails, the browser shows its message, and the `submit` event never fires, so your handler only ever sees forms that passed.

The same checks are open to scripts, through the **Constraint Validation API**. `input.validity` is an object of booleans saying what's wrong, like `valueMissing` or `tooShort`. `form.checkValidity()` answers whether every field passes. `input.setCustomValidity("That name is taken")` marks a field invalid with your own message, and an empty string clears it. `form.reportValidity()` shows the messages now. And as the forms lesson said, the server checks again, always.

## Don't send twice

A slow request invites a second click, and a second note. Set the submit button's `disabled` property to `true` while the request runs, and back to `false` when it's done. A `finally` block, after `try` and `catch`, runs either way, so it's the place to turn the button back on.

## Progressive enhancement

Give the form an `action` and a `method` anyway, so it still works the ordinary way if the script fails to load, as long as the server handles a normal form submit too, the way the forms lesson described. The script then takes over when it can. That's the progressive enhancement from the forms lesson: a page that works without JavaScript, and is better with it.

## Cancelling and timeouts

Sometimes an answer is no longer wanted. In a search box that searches as you type, a slow answer for wat could arrive after the answer for water and replace it. An **AbortController**, from the previous lesson's listener options, cancels a request too:

```javascript
const controller = new AbortController();
fetch("/api/notes?q=water", { signal: controller.signal });
controller.abort();
```

Calling `abort()` makes that `fetch` reject with an error named `AbortError`, which your `catch` can recognize and ignore.

`fetch` has no time limit of its own, and on a bad connection it can wait for minutes. `AbortSignal.timeout(8000)` is a signal that aborts by itself after 8 seconds, and its error is named `TimeoutError`, so `{ signal: AbortSignal.timeout(8000) }` puts a limit on any request.

examples.title: Saving a note
examples.prompt: A function that sends a new note as JSON, called twice: once with text, and once with an empty string, which the server refuses.
examples.output:
Saved note 3: Pack snacks
The server answered 400
examples.explanation: `addNote` sends a POST with a JSON body and returns the promise from `response.json()`, so `await addNote(...)` gives the saved note. The server gave it id 3, after the two it started with. The empty note fails the server's own check, so it answers `400 Bad Request`, `ok` is `false`, and `addNote` throws, which the `try` and `catch` in `main` handle. `main` exists only so there's an `async` function to `await` in. The server keeps notes in memory, so reload the page and the first call saves note 4, and restarting the server starts the count again.

examples.title: A form that sends in the background
examples.prompt: The page has a form with the class new-note, holding a required text field named text and a button, and a message paragraph. Here, Buy a map was typed and the button pressed.
examples.explanation: The listener is an `async` arrow function, so it can `await` inside. `preventDefault()` keeps the page where it is. FormData reads the field by its name, the button is turned off, and a saving message appears, all before the request starts, so the person sees it at once. When the note is saved, `form.reset()` empties the field. Whether it worked or not, `finally` turns the button back on. Pressing the button with the field empty prints nothing at all: the field is `required`, so the browser shows its own message and never fires `submit`. Giving the message paragraph `role="status"` makes screen readers announce each new message.

examples.title: Cancelling a search nobody needs
examples.prompt: Each search cancels the one before it. Two searches start one after the other, the way fast typing would start them.
examples.output:
Cancelled the search for wat
Notes matching water: 1
examples.explanation: `controller` lives outside the function, so each call can see the one before it. The first call starts a request for wat. The second call aborts that controller before starting its own, so the first `fetch` rejects with an `AbortError`, which the `catch` recognizes and reports. Any other error is thrown again, since it's a real problem. The second search finishes, and one note, Check the weather, contains water. `encodeURIComponent` percent-encodes the search, from the lessons on addresses, so a space or an `&` in it can't break the query string.

steps.title: The same-origin policy and CORS
steps.body:
The first time your page calls an API on another origin, you'll likely meet a red error in the Console that mentions CORS. It's not a bug in your code. It's the browser protecting the people who use it, and the fix belongs on the server. This part explains what's blocked, why, and how a server allows it.

## The same-origin policy

The How the Web Works lessons defined an **origin**: the scheme, the host, and the port of a URL together. `http://localhost:8000` and `http://localhost:8001` are different origins, since their ports differ.

A page's scripts can send requests to any origin, but by default they can only read the answers from their own. That rule is the **same-origin policy**. Here's why it exists. Browsers send cookies with every request to a site, as you learned with HTTP, so if you're logged in to your bank, any request to your bank carries your login. Without the policy, a page in another tab could fetch your bank's account page, with your cookies attached, and read your balance. The policy lets the request go but hides the answer from the other page's code.

## CORS: the server says who may read

**CORS**, short for Cross-Origin Resource Sharing, is how a server lets other origins read its answers. It adds a header to its response:

```http
Access-Control-Allow-Origin: http://localhost:8001
```

The value is one origin, or `*` for any origin at all, which suits public data that needs no login. The browser checks the header against the page's origin. If they match, your code gets the response. If not, `fetch` rejects with a TypeError, and the Console explains why, as the first example shows.

CORS is enforced by browsers alone. curl, and servers calling other servers, ignore it completely. So it doesn't protect your API from anyone: it protects people's data inside their own browser. Your API still needs its own checks on who may do what.

## Preflight requests

Some requests are **simple**: a GET, or a POST with a body of the kinds a plain HTML form can send, and only basic headers. The browser sends those straight away and checks the answer afterwards.

Anything else could do something no plain form ever could: a PUT or a DELETE, a JSON body, or a header like `Authorization`. Before sending one of those to another origin, the browser asks first, with a **preflight**: an `OPTIONS` request saying where it's from and what it wants to send.

```diagram fetch-storage-web-apis-preflight
For a JSON POST to another origin, the browser asks first. Only an allowed answer lets the real request go.
```

In step 1, the browser sends `OPTIONS` with `Origin`, `Access-Control-Request-Method`, and `Access-Control-Request-Headers`. In step 2, the server answers with what it allows: origins, methods, and headers. In step 3, if the real request fits, the browser sends it. In step 4, the answer comes back with `Access-Control-Allow-Origin`, and your code can read it. `Access-Control-Max-Age` lets the browser reuse a preflight's answer for that many seconds instead of asking every time. You can send a preflight yourself, with curl, to see what a server allows:

```bash
curl -i -X OPTIONS http://localhost:8000/api/notes -H "Origin: http://localhost:8001" -H "Access-Control-Request-Method: POST" -H "Access-Control-Request-Headers: content-type"
```

```text
HTTP/1.1 204 No Content
Access-Control-Allow-Origin: http://localhost:8001
Access-Control-Allow-Methods: GET, POST
Access-Control-Allow-Headers: Content-Type
Access-Control-Max-Age: 600
Date: Sat, 21 Nov 2026 22:31:55 GMT
Connection: keep-alive
Keep-Alive: timeout=5
```

`204 No Content` means yes, with nothing in the body. The headers say a page from port 8001 may send GET and POST requests with a `Content-Type` header, and the browser may remember that for ten minutes.

## Cookies across origins

A `fetch` to another origin sends no cookies unless you add `credentials: "include"` to its options. The server then has to answer with `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true` too, and name the exact origin, since `*` isn't allowed when cookies are involved.

## Fixing it

Fix CORS on the server: add the headers, usually with a setting in its framework, which the backend courses show. Allow only the origins that need it. While you develop, you can often avoid the problem entirely with a **dev proxy**: the development server passes requests for `/api` on to the real API, so the page and the API share one origin. The lesson on shipping your code sets one up with Vite.

Never fix it by turning CORS off in your browser with a setting or an extension. That only works on your own computer, and your visitors still see the error.

To try all this, make a second folder, `other-site`, with an `index.html` that loads an `app.js` as a module, and serve it with Python's server on port 8001 while the notes server runs on 8000.

examples.title: Reading from another origin, blocked
examples.prompt: other-site/app.js, on a page served at http://localhost:8001, asks the notes server on port 8000 for its notes. This is what the Console showed.
examples.output:
Access to fetch at 'http://localhost:8000/api/notes' from origin 'http://localhost:8001' has been blocked by CORS policy: No 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin' header is present on the requested resource.
Failed to load resource: net::ERR_FAILED
TypeError: Failed to fetch
examples.explanation: The first two lines come from the browser itself, in red. The first is the one to read: the page's origin, port 8001, isn't the API's, port 8000, and the answer had no `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` header, so the browser hid it. The second is the failed request. The last line is the script's own: `fetch` rejected with a TypeError whose message, Failed to fetch, says nothing about why, which is why the browser's line matters. The request did reach the server, and the server's terminal shows `GET /api/notes`. The server answered as usual: the browser is the one that kept the answer from the page.

examples.title: Letting one origin in
examples.prompt: A function to add to server.mjs, above createServer. Then make it the first thing the request handler does, with if (allowCors(request, response)) return.
examples.explanation: Every response now carries `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` naming port 8001, so a page from there may read the answers, and a page from anywhere else still may not. An `OPTIONS` request is a preflight, so the function answers it on the spot with `204 No Content` and the methods and headers it allows, and returns `true` so the handler stops there. Any other request returns `false` and carries on as before. Restart the server with Ctrl+C and `node server.mjs`, reload the page on port 8001, and the same script prints Loaded 2 notes. Real servers keep the allowed origins in a setting, since the live site's origin differs from your computer's.

examples.title: A preflight, seen from the server
examples.prompt: With allowCors in place, the page on port 8001 sends a new note with a JSON body, like the addNote function in the previous part. This is everything the server's terminal printed.
examples.output:
Notes server on http://localhost:8000
OPTIONS /api/notes
POST /api/notes
examples.explanation: The page made one `fetch` call, but two requests arrived. A JSON body isn't something a plain HTML form can send, so the browser sent an `OPTIONS` preflight first, asking whether port 8001 may POST with a `Content-Type` header. `allowCors` said yes, so the browser sent the real POST, which saved the note, and the page printed the note it got back. Neither request shows in your code, but both show in the Network panel, where the preflight appears as its own row. Send the same request again within ten minutes and only the POST arrives, since `Access-Control-Max-Age` lets the browser remember the answer.

steps.title: Storing data in the browser
steps.body:
Pages often need to remember things between visits: a chosen theme, a half-written message, the items in a cart, whether someone has seen the welcome tour. The browser gives each origin a few places to keep data, and they differ in how long the data lasts, how much fits, and who can see it.

## localStorage

**localStorage** keeps strings under names you choose, for one origin, until something deletes them. It survives reloads, closing the tab, and restarting the computer:

```javascript
localStorage.setItem("theme", "dark");
localStorage.getItem("theme");
localStorage.removeItem("theme");
```

`getItem` gives back the string, or `null` when there's nothing under that name. It only stores strings, so to keep an object or an array, store `JSON.stringify(value)` and read it back with `JSON.parse`. Each origin gets about 5 MB.

Two cautions. Reading and writing localStorage pauses the main thread, so keep what you store small. And any script on your origin can read it, an injected one included, so never keep a password or a login token there. The XSS attack from the previous lesson could read it all.

## sessionStorage

**sessionStorage** works exactly the same way, with one difference: it lasts only as long as the tab. It survives a reload but disappears when the tab closes, and each tab has its own. It's handy for things like a half-filled form, kept for this visit alone.

## Cookies

Cookies, from the How the Web Works lessons, are different: the server usually sets them, with a `Set-Cookie` header, and the browser sends them back with every request to that site. That makes them the place for a **session**, the record that you're logged in. A server sets one like this:

```http
Set-Cookie: session=7f3a9c2e; HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax; Path=/; Max-Age=1209600
```

The parts after the value are **flags**, and they matter for safety:

- `HttpOnly` hides the cookie from JavaScript entirely, so an XSS attack can't steal it. Session cookies should always have it.
- `Secure` sends the cookie only over HTTPS, so nobody on the network can read it. Browsers make an exception for localhost.
- `SameSite=Lax` keeps the cookie off requests that other sites trigger in the background, like a hidden form posting to your site, while still sending it when someone follows a link to you. It's the default in most browsers. `Strict` never sends it from another site, and `None` always does, which requires `Secure`.
- `Max-Age` is how many seconds the cookie lasts, here two weeks. Without it, the cookie is deleted when the browser closes.
- `Path` limits which paths it's sent to, and `/` means the whole site.

Scripts can read and set cookies that aren't `HttpOnly` with `document.cookie`. Reading it gives one string with every cookie, like `a=1; b=2`, and assigning to it sets one cookie at a time, which is awkward. Since every cookie rides along on every request, keep them few and small: about 4 KB each at most.

## Bigger storage

**IndexedDB** is a database inside the browser, for large amounts of structured data: an email app's messages, so they show offline, or the drafts of a long document. Its own methods are long-winded, so most people use a small library over it. The **Cache API** stores whole responses, a page or a picture, and it's what lets a site work offline, with the service workers in the last part of this lesson.

## Limits

Browsers give each origin a share of the disk, and may clear stored data when space runs low. A private window starts empty and forgets everything when it closes. Safari also deletes what scripts stored for a site after about a week of using Safari without visiting it. So treat browser storage as a convenience: anything that must not be lost belongs on a server.

The **Application** panel in Chrome's DevTools shows every kind of storage for the page: localStorage, sessionStorage, cookies with all their flags, and IndexedDB. You can read, edit, and delete entries there, which is the quickest way to test what your page does with an empty storage.

examples.title: Remembering a theme
examples.prompt: A select with the class theme-picker offers Same as device, Light, and Dark. The theme tokens from the CSS lessons follow data-theme on the html element. Here Dark was chosen, then the page was reloaded.
examples.output:
Saved theme: none
Saved theme: dark
examples.explanation: `document.documentElement` is the `html` element, where the CSS lessons put `data-theme`. On the first visit, nothing is stored, `getItem` gives `null`, and `|| ""` turns that into an empty string, which means follow the device. Choosing Dark sets the attribute, so the page turns dark at once, and saves the choice. After the reload, the script finds dark in storage and applies it again, and the select shows it too. A module runs after the page is parsed, so the page can flash the device's theme for a moment first. Sites avoid that with a few lines of the same code in a plain `script` element at the top of the `head`, which runs before the body is drawn.

examples.title: Storing an array as JSON
examples.prompt: The task list from the previous lesson, stored in localStorage and read back.
examples.output:
string
[{"id":1,"text":"Pack water","done":false},{"id":2,"text":"Charge phone","done":true}]
Charge phone true
null
examples.explanation: `JSON.stringify` turns the array into one string of JSON, and that's what gets stored. Reading it back gives the same string, not an array, as `typeof` shows. `JSON.parse` rebuilds the array of objects, so `loaded[1]` works again, with its boolean intact. A name that was never stored gives `null`. In the previous lesson's task app, you'd save the array at the end of `render`, and at the start, use `JSON.parse(localStorage.getItem("tasks"))` when something is stored, so the list survives a reload. Storing `tasks` directly, without `JSON.stringify`, would save the useless string `[object Object],[object Object]`.

examples.title: Setting and reading cookies from a script
examples.prompt: Two cookies set from JavaScript, then one deleted. Each line of the Console shows document.cookie at that moment.
examples.explanation: Each assignment to `document.cookie` sets one cookie, with its flags after the value, and leaves the others alone, even though it looks like it replaces the whole string. `Max-Age=31536000` keeps each one for a year. Reading `document.cookie` gives all of them in one string, names and values only, with no flags. To delete a cookie, set it again with `Max-Age=0` and the same `Path`. Both cookies now travel to the server with every request to this site, which is the point of a cookie: use one when the server needs the value. When only the page does, like the theme, localStorage is simpler and adds nothing to every request.

steps.title: The URL and History APIs
steps.body:
An address should say what's on the screen. Then a filtered search can be shared in a message, a bookmark opens the same tab, and a reload doesn't throw away where you were. The browser gives scripts two tools for that: objects for reading and building URLs, and a way to change the address without loading a new page.

## URL and URLSearchParams

`new URL()` takes an address and splits it into the pieces from the How the Web Works lessons:

- `url.protocol`, `url.hostname`, `url.port`, and `url.origin`
- `url.pathname`, the path
- `url.search`, the query string with its `?`, and `url.hash`, the fragment with its `#`

`url.searchParams` handles the query string for you. `get("q")` reads a value, already decoded, `set("q", "red shoes")` adds or replaces one, `append` adds another with the same name, and `delete` removes one. Turn the URL back into a string with `url.href`, and every value is percent-encoded correctly, so an `&` or a space in a value can't break the address. A relative address needs a base: `new URL("/search", location.href)`.

`new URLSearchParams(text)` does the same for a query string alone, like `new URLSearchParams(location.search)`.

## location

`location` is the current page's address, as an object with the same pieces: `location.href`, `location.pathname`, `location.search`, and `location.hash`. Assigning to `location.href`, or calling `location.assign(url)`, loads another page, like following a link, and `location.reload()` loads this one again.

## Changing the address without loading

`history.pushState(state, "", url)` changes the address in the address bar, and adds an entry to the tab's history, without loading anything. The page stays exactly as it is, and the request a link would normally make never happens. The first argument is any data you want to keep with that entry, often `null`, and the second is unused, so pass an empty string.

`history.replaceState()` does the same, but replaces the current entry instead of adding one. Use it for changes that shouldn't each be a step back, like the text in a filter box, which would otherwise add one history entry per keystroke.

```diagram fetch-storage-web-apis-push-state
The address changes three times, and the page is loaded only once.
```

In the diagram, the page loads once, at the top. Clicking Map and then List calls `pushState` twice, so the address changes and the history grows, while the same page stays loaded and the script swaps what it shows. The network sees one request for the page.

## Going back: popstate

When someone presses Back or Forward through entries your script made, the browser changes the address and fires a **popstate** event on `window`. It doesn't change the page for you, so your listener reads `location` and shows the matching view. `pushState` itself never fires `popstate`: only moving through the history does.

## Single-page apps

Put those together and you get a **single-page app**, or SPA: the server sends one page and its JavaScript, and from then on, clicking a link calls `preventDefault()`, then `pushState`, then renders the new view, with data from `fetch` when needed. Moving around feels instant, since no page loads. React Router, in the React course, works this way.

One catch: the addresses must work when opened fresh too. If someone reloads `/trails/42`, the browser asks the server for that path, and a server that only knows `/` answers 404. So the server for an SPA answers every app path with the same page, and the script reads `location` to decide what to show. A newer **Navigation API** handles all of this through one event, and has worked in every current browser since early 2026, so you'll start to see it in libraries.

examples.title: Reading and building an address
examples.prompt: The shop address from the lesson on web addresses, split into its pieces, then changed through searchParams.
examples.explanation: Each property is one piece of the address. `searchParams.get("q")` decodes the value for you, turning the `+` back into a space, and gives back a string, so `size` is the string `"9"`, not a number. Setting `q` to a value with spaces and an `&` in it, then printing `href`, shows the encoding done for you: spaces became `+` and the `&` became `%26`, so it can't be mistaken for the start of another value. `size` is gone, and the fragment stayed where it was. Building addresses by joining strings yourself is how query strings get broken, and this way they never are.

examples.title: A filter kept in the address
examples.prompt: A search field with the class filter. As you type, the address's q value follows it. Here the page was opened, water was typed, and the page was reloaded.
examples.output:
Filter on load: none
Filter on load: water
examples.explanation: On the first load, the address has no `q`, so the field starts empty. Each keystroke builds a new URL from the current one, sets or deletes `q`, and swaps it in with `replaceState`, so the address bar ends at `?q=water` without five steps of history for Back to wade through. Reloading sends that address to the server, and the script reads `q` back out of `location.search` and fills in the field, which is the second line. Copy the address into a message, and whoever opens it sees the same filtered list. A real page would also filter the list itself, from the same value.

examples.title: Views that work with Back
examples.prompt: Two links, List and Map, each with a data-view and an href with a query string. Here Map and then List were clicked, then Back was pressed twice.
examples.output:
Showing the list (no query)
Showing the map (?view=map)
Showing the list (?view=list)
Showing the map (?view=map)
Showing the list (no query)
examples.explanation: The last line of the script shows the list when the page loads. Each click is caught by a delegated listener: `preventDefault()` stops the link from loading a page, `pushState` puts the link's address in the bar, and `show` changes the heading. Back fires `popstate`, the listener reads the view from the address, and the page shows it again: first the map, then the list with no query, where it started. The page loaded only once in all of this. They're real links with real addresses, so a middle-click still opens a view in a new tab, and the page works without the script too.

steps.title: More browser APIs

examples.title: Searching when typing stops
examples.prompt: A search field with the class search. Here water was typed quickly, then after a pause, an s was added.
examples.output:
Searching for water
Searching for waters
examples.explanation: Every keystroke fires `input`. The listener cancels the timer from the keystroke before, then starts a new one for 300 milliseconds. While you type quickly, each timer is cancelled before it runs, so nothing happens. Only when you pause for 300 milliseconds does a timer survive and run its search, with the whole word. Typing water made five `input` events and one search, and the s after the pause made one more. In a real page, the search would call the `fetch` with an AbortController from the second part, so the server gets a request per pause, not per letter.

examples.title: Noticing the end of a list
examples.prompt: At the bottom of a long list sits a paragraph with the class load-more. The page was opened, then scrolled to the end.
examples.output:
Marker on screen: false
Marker on screen: true
examples.explanation: `new IntersectionObserver` takes a callback, and `observe` names an element to watch. The callback gets a list of entries, one for each watched element that changed, and `isIntersecting` says whether it's on screen now. The first line comes straight away, as the observer reports where the marker starts: below the screen. The second comes when scrolling brings it into view. That's where a page would fetch the next results and add them to the list. The browser does the watching, so there's no work on every scroll, unlike a `scroll` listener that measures positions over and over.

examples.title: Heavy work on another thread
examples.prompt: The page's module starts primes-worker.js, shown above, asks it to count the prime numbers below five million, and listens for the answer.
examples.output:
Counting in the background. The page still responds.
Primes below 5000000: 348513
examples.explanation: `new Worker` starts the script on a thread of its own, and `type: "module"` lets it use modules. `postMessage` sends it the number, and the worker's `message` listener gets it as `event.data`. The page's script carries on at once and prints its first line. The worker checks millions of numbers, which takes a moment, then sends back its count, which arrives as a `message` event on the page. On the main thread, that loop would be one long task, and the page would freeze until it ended. In a worker, scrolling and clicking carry on while it counts.

recap:
- fetch returns a promise, await waits for it inside an async function, and response.json() reads the body.
- fetch only rejects when no answer arrives, so check response.ok, and show loading and error states.
- Send JSON with method, headers, and body, take over a form with preventDefault and FormData, and cancel with an AbortController.
- The same-origin policy hides other origins' answers, and CORS headers on the server let chosen origins read them, after a preflight for anything a form couldn't send.
- localStorage keeps strings per origin, sessionStorage lasts as long as the tab, and session cookies belong in HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookies.
- URL and URLSearchParams build addresses safely, and pushState with popstate changes the address without loading a page.
- Timers, observers, workers, and live connections cover most of what else a page needs, and MDN documents them all.
